subject: INLA crashes for a large dataset in a simple model

messages.author: d801fdf2fefdd38e
messages.subject: INLA crashes for a large dataset in a simple model
parts:
Hi,
I'm running a relatively simple mixed effects model in R, but I have a large dataset (n=300,000), which will get larger when we include the full dataset. When I run this on an HPC without using GPUs and only 16 GB RAM, the model completes in about 20 minutes. But when my colleague runs it on a Windows computer it crashes with the error message pasted below. 
I can't share the dataset, but I've simulated some data that look similar to what we have. 
I'm wondering if there are some changes I can make to the code that will allow this to run more smoothly on a standard computer. Our final dataset could contain millions of observations, and we are able to let the model run for a long time. 
Thank you,
Mikey

#----- Here is the code to simulate data and run the model
```
library(INLA)

# simulate some data for a reproducible example
set.seed(123)
n <- 300000
y <- rbinom(n, 1, .3) # target obersvations 
id <- sample(paste0('ind', 1:15), size=n, replace=TRUE) # individual names
# variables
NHDP <- runif(n, min=-2, max=2)
DecMix <- runif(n, min=-2, max=1)
ValSlo <- runif(n, min=-1, max=2)
EVI <- runif(n, min=0, max=2)

# organize data for INLA and scale covariates
dat2 <- data.frame(
  y=y,
  id=id,
  NHDP=scale(NHDP),
  DecMix=scale(DecMix),
  ValSlo=scale(ValSlo),
  EVI=scale(EVI)
)

# convert individual IDs into integers for INLA
rsf <- transform(dat2, id=match(id, unique(id)))

# create a separate ID variable with different names for each random effect
rsf$id0 <- rsf$id1 <- rsf$id2 <- rsf$id3 <- rsf$id

# generate a weights variable: weighting 0s by 1000
rsf$weights <- ifelse(rsf$y==1, 1, 1000)

# allow INLA to use weights
inla.setOption("enable.inla.argument.weights", TRUE)
#INLA:::inla.dynload.workaround() # when using HPC

# specify formula.
formula <- y ~ NHDP + ValSlo + DecMix + EVI +
  f(id, model = "iid", # random intercepts
    hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1e-6), # variance of intercepts is 10^6. This is specified as the log of the precision
                              fixed = TRUE))) +
  f(id0, NHDP, values = 1:max(rsf$id), # values are all of the individuals (we want a random effect for each ind)
    model = "iid",
    hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1), fixed = FALSE, # initial variance of 1 and is not fixed
                              prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, .05) # this is a PC prior
    ))) +
  f(id1, ValSlo, values = 1:max(rsf$id), model="iid", 
    hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1), fixed = FALSE,
                              prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, .05))) ) +
  f(id2, DecMix, values = 1:max(rsf$id), model="iid", 
    hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1), fixed = FALSE,
                              prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, .05))) ) +
  f(id3, EVI, values = 1:max(rsf$id), model="iid", 
    hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1), fixed = FALSE,
                              prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, .05))) )

# fit model
glmm <- inla(formula, weights=rsf$weights,
             family = "binomial", data = rsf, verbose = TRUE)
```

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA crashes for a large dataset in a simple model
parts:
Hi,

there are several reports that Windows do not handle larger models, and
I have no idea why. Also when its reported that a virt-machine with
Linux, on the same Windows machine, runs larger models fine. If anyone
have any idea why, please let us know.

If you want to go higher in dimension, you can check out

inla.pardiso()

and especially the 'pardiso.paralle' strategy, which might be needed if
you go high. also use the mkl version, like with

inla.setOption(mkl=TRUE)

on Linux, for sure...

H

On Tue, 2020-05-05 at 03:15 -0700, Mikey T wrote:
> > Hi,
>
> I'm running a relatively simple mixed effects model in R, but I have
> a large dataset (n=300,000), which will get larger when we include
> the full dataset. When I run this on an HPC without using GPUs and
> only 16 GB RAM, the model completes in about 20 minutes. But when my
> colleague runs it on a Windows computer it crashes with the error
> message pasted below.
> I can't share the dataset, but I've simulated some data that look
> similar to what we have.
> I'm wondering if there are some changes I can make to the code that
> will allow this to run more smoothly on a standard computer. Our
> final dataset could contain millions of observations, and we are able
> to let the model run for a long time.
> Thank you,
> Mikey
>
> #----- Here is the code to simulate data and run the model
> ```
> library(INLA)
>
> # simulate some data for a reproducible example
> set.seed(123)
> n <- 300000
> y <- rbinom(n, 1, .3) # target obersvations
> id <- sample(paste0('ind', 1:15), size=n, replace=TRUE) # individual
> names
> # variables
> NHDP <- runif(n, min=-2, max=2)
> DecMix <- runif(n, min=-2, max=1)
> ValSlo <- runif(n, min=-1, max=2)
> EVI <- runif(n, min=0, max=2)
>
> # organize data for INLA and scale covariates
> dat2 <- data.frame(
> y=y,
> id=id,
> NHDP=scale(NHDP),
> DecMix=scale(DecMix),
> ValSlo=scale(ValSlo),
> EVI=scale(EVI)
> )
>
> # convert individual IDs into integers for INLA
> rsf <- transform(dat2, id=match(id, unique(id)))
>
> # create a separate ID variable with different names for each random
> effect
> rsf$id0 <- rsf$id1 <- rsf$id2 <- rsf$id3 <- rsf$id
>
> # generate a weights variable: weighting 0s by 1000
> rsf$weights <- ifelse(rsf$y==1, 1, 1000)
>
> # allow INLA to use weights
> inla.setOption("enable.inla.argument.weights", TRUE)
> #INLA:::inla.dynload.workaround() # when using HPC
>
> # specify formula.
> formula <- y ~ NHDP + ValSlo + DecMix + EVI +
> f(id, model = "iid", # random intercepts
> hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1e-6), # variance of
> intercepts is 10^6. This is specified as the log of the precision
> fixed = TRUE))) +
> f(id0, NHDP, values = 1:max(rsf$id), # values are all of the
> individuals (we want a random effect for each ind)
> model = "iid",
> hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1), fixed = FALSE, #
> initial variance of 1 and is not fixed
> prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, .05) #
> this is a PC prior
> ))) +
> f(id1, ValSlo, values = 1:max(rsf$id), model="iid",
> hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1), fixed = FALSE,
> prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, .05)))
> ) +
> f(id2, DecMix, values = 1:max(rsf$id), model="iid",
> hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1), fixed = FALSE,
> prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, .05)))
> ) +
> f(id3, EVI, values = 1:max(rsf$id), model="iid",
> hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1), fixed = FALSE,
> prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, .05)))
> )
>
> # fit model
> glmm <- inla(formula, weights=rsf$weights,
> family = "binomial", data = rsf, verbose = TRUE)
> ```

parts:
Every platform has some quirks with INLA: I have had models that run only on Windows and others that have worked much better on Linux.  A few things that jump out at me for your model, in terms of possible tweaks:

 

  1. Ensure that BLAS threads are limited to 1 (this is primarily a Linux concern), and always consider capping num.threads (this is for the whole process, not just BLAS) at a number that leaves a few cores / threads open for the OS / non-INLA programs to run.  The former can help performance, particularly with OpenBLAS; the latter helps avoid crashes, especially on Windows, caused by overloading resources. In response to H’s question, I assume, but don’t know for sure, that these crashes sometimes happen on Windows  if you have too many threads because you end up using too much memory.  Anyway, start with num.thread = 1 and work your way up if need be.
  2. Consider using “eb” as your integration strategy: once you get over 100k observations it generally makes little difference anyway, and this allows you to tackle larger datasets with more detailed latent structures.
  3. If you can avoid making predictions that helps a lot.  Plenty of models that crash are doing fine until the burden of making the predictions (or encountering bad NA values for predictors in the prediction set)  brings them down.  It looks like you currently aren’t calling for predictions, though, and yours is failing pretty early on.
  4. Adding weights can multiply the number of effective observations tremendously, making the dataset harder to handle.  Using the weights argument with INLA also seems to be dangerous (it consistently gives me nonsense results, at least with continuous distributions), and I don’t see why it is being used here.  With a binomial model, doesn’t it make more sense just to use “NTrials”? INLA handles that argument without any problem and seems to scale quite well with it.
  5. INLA creates a lot of temp files; if you are low on disk space this can create issues. 

 

With all of this said, I tried your model in Windows and it still crashed on me.  So there may just be something about the way the data is structured in this particular model.  Does it work fine in, say, lme4?

 

Jonathan

there are several reports that Windows do not handle larger models, and

and especially the 'pardiso.paralle' strategy, which might be needed if

you go high. also use the mkl version, like with

 

                inla.setOption(mkl=TRUE)
